paras: The attempted lynching of Oscar Bates took place at the Good Times Inn in Comfort, Texas, on or shortly before August 20, 1905, when armed German citizens came for Bates, a Black dishwasher accused of insulting a local girl. Bates escaped under gunfire, and the inn's Black staff then left Comfort for San Antonio, leaving the town without Black residents.

The Good Times Inn at Comfort, run by a manager named Stanley, had fifty or sixty guests and a Black staff that included Bates, a cook and a waiter. Bates was accused of insulting the daughter of a German citizen who lived near the inn.

According to a San Antonio dispatch, eight "enraged German citizens, armed with guns," went to the inn, demanded the dishwasher and took him to the woods, where "he escaped in some manner unknown." Gunshots were heard from the woods. Mitchell Garcia, a co-worker, said instead that the men demanded Bates give himself up, and he ran down the railroad track while two shots were fired at him.

Bates and six others, including Garcia and his wife, reached San Antonio on August 20. Garcia said they left because "we were not satisfied with the protection offered to us," and that their departure "cleaned the town of colored people." Stanley hired replacement staff from San Antonio, and no report of an arrest or prosecution appears in the coverage.

The San Antonio wire, printed on August 22 by the Palestine Daily Herald and the Bryan Morning Eagle under "NEGRO ESCAPED," gave the alleged insult as the cause and its second paragraph to guests who found helping with Sunday dinner "a great lark." The San Antonio Daily Light, a day earlier, printed Garcia's account at length, calling the insult "alleged" and quoting his view that the men "took snap judgment over Bates."
No Black-press coverage of the episode was found.
The wire, which names no source, says Bates was taken to the woods and escaped by unknown means; Garcia, one of the Black staff, says he fled down the railroad track before he could be seized.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Oscar Bates
bases: Armed white men seized or demanded a Black dishwasher accused of insulting a white girl with, in the wire's words, intent to lynch him, and fired at him as he escaped; no one was killed (A1, A2, A3).

A group of eight armed men (A2, A3), or 'a lot of men' (A1), acting without authority over an alleged insult tried to lynch Bates, but he escaped and no death is reported, so this was an attempted lynching rather than a lynching (A1, A2).

The San Antonio wire (A2, A3) and the Daily Light's separate interview with Garcia (A1) agree that local men came for the dishwasher over an alleged insult, that he got away, and that shots were fired, though they differ on how he escaped.

accounts.label: Wire report
accounts.gist: Eight enraged, armed German citizens demanded and got the dishwasher, took him to the woods intending to lynch him, and he escaped 'in some manner unknown' while shots were heard.

accounts.label: Mitchell Garcia (Black co-worker)
accounts.gist: Men demanded that Bates come out and give himself up; he ran down the railroad track instead and two shots were fired at him; the Black staff left for lack of protection.

framing.detail: The wire ran under 'NEGRO ESCAPED. Eight Germans Intended to Lynch Dishwasher,' gave the alleged insult as the cause, and spent its second paragraph on guests finding kitchen work 'a great lark.'
The San Antonio Daily Light called the accusation an 'alleged insult' and let Garcia argue the men took 'snap judgment,' while using 'darky' in his quoted words and 'French leave' for the departure.

versions.value: Seized at the inn, taken to the woods, escaped by unknown means; shots heard from the woods
Ordered to come out and surrender, he ran down the railroad track; two shots fired at him

conflicts.note: Garcia's is a firsthand account from the Black staff, relayed by a local paper; the wire names no source and admits it does not know how he escaped.
The accounts are compatible; only the wire gives a number.

sources.paper: San Antonio Daily Light (San Antonio, Tex.)
sources.note: Local interview with Mitchell Garcia, one of the Black workers who left Comfort; names Oscar Bates as the accused, says he fled down the railroad track and two shots were fired at him.
quotes: We left Comfort because we were not satisfied with the protection offered to us.
We think they took snap judgment over Bates, as we didn't think he meant to be disrespectful to the young lady.
There were two shots fired at Oscar Bates as he was making a hot-foot down the track.
